paragraphs: Data valuation asks how much a data source contributes to a model’s predictive behavior. Existing approaches typically assume that sources share either the same features or the same samples. This paper addresses a more fragmented situation: each source may provide only some features for some samples, so its contribution occupies only part of the combined data matrix.

The authors first develop a way to calculate the counterfactual outcome of removing one such fragment. This gives a basis for assessing what that fragment contributes when combined with other available data. They then introduce 2D-Shapley, a valuation framework that uniquely satisfies a specified set of axioms for this fragmented setting.

The framework makes it possible to evaluate contributions at a finer level than an entire sample or source. Its stated uses include choosing useful fragments, explaining sample-level valuations, and locating data problems more precisely. The theoretical uniqueness claim is tied to the framework’s axioms, giving a principled basis for valuation within that formulation.
icml-2023-2d-shapley-a-framework-for-fra.tldr: 2D-Shapley provides an axiomatic way to value data sources that contain only partial sets of both samples and features.

paragraphs: A private histogram must protect all records belonging to any one user, even when some users contribute far more records than others. Because the required noise grows with the largest contribution, a few unusually prolific users can substantially reduce accuracy. Capping contributions controls that noise, but setting the cap too low discards useful data.

This paper develops algorithms for selecting the contribution cap in two settings. For a bounded domain, the proposed strategy nearly achieves a two-approximation relative to the best cap chosen with hindsight. For an unbounded domain, it provides a logarithmic approximation relative to that hindsight choice, without assuming a particular data distribution.

These guarantees address the practical trade-off between privacy noise and information lost through clipping. Experiments on real and synthetic data support the theoretical findings and the algorithms’ effectiveness. The authors also show that clipping bias may be reduced under mild distribution assumptions; that additional result has assumptions distinct from the distribution-free unbounded-domain approximation guarantee.
icml-2023-algorithms-for-bounding-contri.tldr: The paper develops principled contribution caps that balance discarded data against privacy noise when estimating user-private histograms.

paragraphs: Bi-level optimization links an upper-level objective to a lower-level optimization problem. Existing gradient methods often rely on strong convexity of the lower problem, highly accurate solutions to repeated approximation subproblems, or both. These requirements can make the methods restrictive or expensive when applied to large learning problems.

The paper proposes sl-BAMM, a single-loop method of multipliers built by averaging the upper- and lower-level objectives. It removes the requirement that the lower-level objective be strongly convex. The single-loop design is intended to provide a simple and efficient approach for large-scale bi-level optimization.

The authors give a non-asymptotic convergence analysis toward KKT stationary points, a stationarity target rather than a claim of global optimality. Their analysis also avoids a strong bounded-gradient assumption used in previous work. This broadens the applications covered by the theory, particularly cases where the upper objective is quadratic in the lower-level variable. Reported experiments support the method’s comparative advantages.
icml-2023-averaged-method-of-multipliers.tldr: sl-BAMM offers single-loop bi-level optimization with convergence analysis that avoids lower-level strong convexity and a strong bounded-gradient assumption.

paragraphs: Learning causal structure can benefit from data collected under different conditions, including both ordinary observations and interventions. In changing time series, however, the labels identifying those conditions may be missing. Without them, a method has difficulty distinguishing changes caused by interventions from observations generated under other conditions.

The proposed Latent Intervened Non-stationary learning method, LIN, couples recovery of these hidden domain labels with causal structure learning. Rather than treating the recovered labels as a completely separate input, the approach lets the two learning processes support each other. Information about the causal structure helps recover domains, while the recovered domains help reveal causal structure.

The authors formulate and justify a possible faithfulness condition under which LIN is identifiable. The guarantee therefore depends on that condition; it does not establish unrestricted causal recovery from any changing time series. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show better causal structure learning than the tested baselines in the latent-intervention setting.
icml-2023-causal-structure-learning-for-.tldr: LIN jointly recovers hidden domain labels and causal structure from changing time series, with identifiability guaranteed under a stated faithfulness condition.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether a diffusion model contains small groups of neurons associated with particular subjects. The authors call these groups concept neurons and identify them through statistics of network gradients produced by stimulation connected to a subject. The aim is both to interpret how subjects are represented and to control their appearance in generated images.

The identified neurons provide a direct handle for customization. The authors report that shutting off a subject’s concept neurons can produce that subject in different scenes. Combining several clusters can bring their associated subjects into a single image, with reported success on customization involving four or more subjects.

The representation also reduces storage needs: a customized subject is stored as a sparse collection of integer neuron indices instead of dense floating-point parameters. The abstract reports a 90% storage reduction relative to previous customization methods. Qualitative and quantitative evaluations across diverse scenarios support the approach’s usefulness for interpreting diffusion models and manipulating their outputs.
icml-2023-cones-concept-neurons-in-diffu.tldr: Cones identifies small neuron clusters that support subject-specific diffusion customization and multi-subject generation while substantially reducing storage.

paragraphs: Offline safe reinforcement learning asks an agent to learn useful behavior that respects constraints using an existing dataset. The challenge includes balancing task performance against safety without collecting new training experience through interaction. This paper studies that balance through a multi-objective optimization perspective and introduces epsilon-reducibility as a concept for characterizing problem difficulty.

The resulting method, the constrained decision transformer, is designed to adjust the balance between reward and constraints during deployment. This matters when the acceptable constraint threshold changes after training. Instead of being tied to one fixed operating point, the learned policy retains the ability to adapt to different thresholds without additional training.

The reported experiments find that CDT learns policies combining high reward with safety, robustness, and adaptability. It substantially outperforms its variants and strong offline safe reinforcement learning baselines while using the same hyperparameters across tasks. These findings support flexible deployment under different constraints, with the demonstrated zero-shot threshold adaptation being a central benefit.
icml-2023-constrained-decision-transform.tldr: CDT learns constrained policies from offline data and can adjust the reward–safety trade-off to new constraint thresholds during deployment.

paragraphs: Deep graph clustering groups graph nodes into separate clusters using learned representations. Scaling this process is difficult when graphs contain millions of nodes. Dink-Net addresses the problem by joining representation learning and cluster optimization in one end-to-end framework, so the features being learned are directly shaped by the clustering task.

The method first learns representations through a self-supervised task that distinguishes nodes corrupted by augmentations. Cluster centers are represented as learnable neural parameters. Two objectives, called cluster dilation and cluster shrink losses, then optimize the clustering distribution in an adversarial manner. Their design allows optimization using mini-batches rather than requiring the entire graph at once.

The paper reports that this mini-batch approach scales without performance degradation in its evaluations, supported by experiments and theoretical analysis. On ogbn-papers100M, containing 111 million nodes and 1.6 billion edges, Dink-Net achieves a reported 9.62% NMI improvement over the runner-up. The result connects the method’s scalability goal to clustering quality on a particularly large graph.
icml-2023-dink-net-neural-clustering-on-.tldr: Dink-Net combines representation learning and mini-batch cluster optimization to perform neural clustering on graphs with more than a hundred million nodes.

paragraphs: Retrosynthetic planning seeks a complete sequence of reactions connecting starting materials to a desired molecule. Existing approaches commonly combine a single-step reactant predictor with a separate search algorithm. When each prediction uses only the current product, it leaves out information available elsewhere along the developing synthetic route.

FusionRetro represents routes as reaction graphs so that this broader context can inform reactant predictions. Its pipeline encodes molecules as embeddings, aggregates information across routes, and uses the resulting representations to predict reactants. The framework can be optimized end to end, connecting molecule representation learning directly to the context-aware prediction task.

The authors describe this as an initial use of in-context learning for retrosynthesis prediction within planning. Experiments show significant planning improvements over baselines that do not use route context, particularly for long synthetic routes. The stated findings suggest that considering how reactions fit into a larger route can produce more practical and accurate predictions than evaluating each product in isolation.
icml-2023-fusionretro-molecule-represent.tldr: FusionRetro improves retrosynthetic planning by combining molecular representations with context from the surrounding reaction route.

paragraphs: Private synthetic data aims to reproduce statistical properties of sensitive data while providing differential privacy. Many existing methods optimize the synthetic dataset using gradients. This makes them dependent on differentiable objectives and has limited their success largely to particular statistical queries, such as marginals over discrete attributes.

One workaround is to replace an unsuitable objective with a differentiable approximation, but changing the objective introduces another source of error. Private-GSD takes a different optimization route: it uses a private genetic algorithm based on zeroth-order heuristics. Because the procedure does not require derivatives, it can work with the original objective without modifying it to enable gradient calculations.

The authors evaluate the approach on data containing both discrete and real-valued attributes. They report better performance than state-of-the-art methods on non-differentiable queries, while matching accuracy on differentiable queries. The empirical contribution is therefore broader query support without sacrificing the reported accuracy on objectives already suited to first-order optimization.
icml-2023-generating-private-synthetic-d.tldr: Private-GSD uses genetic optimization to generate differentially private synthetic data without requiring differentiable statistical objectives.

paragraphs: Monte Carlo dropout provides a relatively inexpensive way to approximate Bayesian inference and estimate neural-network uncertainty. Traditional dropout draws masks independently from a fixed distribution. Treating masks as hidden variables to infer offers more flexibility, but learning their distribution introduces difficulties that simple variational approximations may struggle to handle.

The paper highlights two such difficulties. Many quite different masks can be plausible, giving the posterior distribution multiple modes. In addition, information specific to an input and correlations among masks are difficult to exploit fully. GFlowOut uses Generative Flow Networks to learn a posterior distribution over dropout masks and address these issues.

The reported experiments show predictive distributions that generalize better to data outside the training distribution. They also show that the resulting uncertainty estimates improve performance on downstream tasks. These are empirical findings about prediction and uncertainty quality, supporting learned mask distributions as a useful alternative to drawing every mask from the same fixed rule.
icml-2023-gflowout-dropout-with-generati.tldr: GFlowOut learns dropout-mask distributions with Generative Flow Networks, improving reported out-of-distribution prediction and uncertainty-based downstream performance.

paragraphs: Switching dynamical systems describe complicated behavior through simpler modes and transitions between those modes. Existing approaches can discover these patterns from time series, but commonly treat objects as independent: one object’s mode does not depend on the modes of others. That leaves out interactions that can shape how a system changes over time.

GRASS extends this setting to interacting objects whose dynamics depend on an unknown, changing subset of other objects and their modes. It uses a dynamic graph to represent those relationships. The model learns both switching within individual objects and switching behavior involving interactions between objects, making the changing relationships part of the modeling problem.

For evaluation, the authors introduce a synthetic particle dataset driven by ordinary differential equations and a real-world dataset of salsa couples dancing. Experiments report consistent improvements over previous state-of-the-art methods. The contribution is a way to learn changing behavioral modes together with changing interactions, rather than modeling each object’s transitions independently.
icml-2023-graph-switching-dynamical-syst.tldr: GRASS uses a dynamic graph to learn behavioral modes and mode changes in systems of interacting objects.

paragraphs: Programmatic reinforcement learning represents behavior through programs, aiming for policies that people can interpret and that generalize to new situations. The earlier LEAPS approach searches a learned embedding space of programs. Its available policies are constrained by the program dataset, and judging each candidate only by its total return makes it difficult to credit useful parts.

HPRL introduces a meta-policy that composes a sequence of programs sampled from that embedding space. Learning how to combine programs lets the resulting policy express behaviors more complex than those represented in the original program distribution. It also allows credit to be assigned directly to programs that produce desired behavior.

The authors evaluate the framework in the Karel domain and report improvements over the tested baselines. Ablation studies support both their diagnosis of LEAPS’s limitations and their design choices. The central idea is to expand what learned program components can accomplish through composition while giving the learning process more specific feedback about which components help.
icml-2023-hierarchical-programmatic-rein.tldr: HPRL learns to compose program components into more complex policies while assigning credit to components that produce useful behavior.

paragraphs: This paper studies convergence guarantees that hold with a chosen high probability for stochastic gradient methods under sub-Gaussian noise. Such guarantees describe reliability beyond average behavior. For convex optimization, the authors replace dependence on the full domain’s diameter with dependence on the initial distance to an optimal solution.

Their general approach covers Lipschitz objectives, smooth objectives, and linear combinations of the two, using step sizes analogous to standard choices. It also applies to non-convex optimization. For stochastic gradient descent, the paper gives improved bounds for both a known iteration budget and an unknown one, explicitly accounting for the desired success probability.

The authors also provide a new high-probability analysis of AdaGrad-Norm without the bounded-gradient assumption used in previous analyses, and report per-coordinate AdaGrad results in the full version. The contribution is a set of sharper theoretical guarantees under stated noise conditions, with less restrictive assumptions in the adaptive-method analysis and more localized dependence in the convex bounds.
icml-2023-high-probability-convergence-o.tldr: The paper derives improved high-probability convergence bounds for stochastic gradient methods under sub-Gaussian noise, including less restrictive AdaGrad analysis.

paragraphs: When rewards are sparse, a team of reinforcement-learning agents receives little feedback about productive behavior. This paper examines the problem through lazy agents and empirically shows how they can harm both exploration and exploitation. It studies laziness through the causal relationship between agents’ actions and changes in external states.

The proposed LAIES framework uses a causal graph to examine causes and types of laziness. It mathematically defines fully lazy agents and teams using the causal effects of their actions, calculated through do-calculus. An external-state transition model then supports counterfactual reasoning about how actions influence the environment.

LAIES uses that reasoning to construct two intrinsic rewards: one for individual diligence and another for collaborative diligence. These provide learning signals aimed at motivating both agents and teams when task rewards are scarce. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance across several tasks, including sparse-reward versions of StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge and Google Research Football, supporting the usefulness of causally motivated activity signals.
icml-2023-lazy-agents-a-new-perspective-.tldr: LAIES addresses sparse team rewards by rewarding individual and collaborative causal influence on external states.

paragraphs: Neural operators learn mappings between functions in partial differential equation problems. Physical measurements, however, are often distributed unevenly across space. This creates difficulties for mesh-based computational techniques such as the fast Fourier transform, which are easier to use when data is arranged on regular grids.

NUNO addresses this mismatch by decomposing the domain with a K-D tree and converting non-uniform data into uniform grids. The framework controls interpolation error during this transformation. Its purpose is to make efficient operator-learning techniques usable with irregularly distributed physical data while preserving accuracy through the conversion.

The evaluation covers two-dimensional elasticity, channel flow with two spatial dimensions and time, and a three-dimensional multiphysics heatsink. These tasks include complex three-dimensional geometry. The authors report error reductions of up to 60% and training speed improvements ranging from 2 to 30 times. Those results demonstrate the framework’s potential to improve both accuracy and computation in the evaluated PDE-learning settings.
icml-2023-nuno-a-general-framework-for-l.tldr: NUNO converts unevenly distributed physical data into controlled-error uniform grids to improve neural-operator accuracy and training speed.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate high-quality outputs, but generation requires many neural-network evaluations. This paper explores which model should perform each generation step. The authors observe that a smaller model can outperform a larger one at certain steps even when the smaller model produces worse results when used for the entire process.

OMS-DPM turns this observation into a scheduling problem. Given a collection of pretrained models and a generation-time budget, a predictor-based search selects a model schedule. Carefully assigning different models to different steps could improve both output quality and speed, rather than relying on one model throughout generation.

Experiments on CIFAR-10, CelebA, ImageNet, and LSUN show schedules that improve quality and speed relative to prior state-of-the-art methods. Applied to public Stable Diffusion checkpoints, the approach doubles sampling speed while maintaining generation quality. These findings support model selection across steps as a useful additional way to optimize the cost of diffusion generation.
icml-2023-oms-dpm-optimizing-the-model-s.tldr: OMS-DPM searches for step-specific combinations of pretrained diffusion models to improve generation quality and speed within a time budget.

paragraphs: The paper develops a method for estimating population quantiles under local differential privacy using binary inquiries. Its goal includes both producing an estimate and quantifying the uncertainty around it. This is useful when a private analysis needs a confidence interval, rather than only a single reported quantile.

The algorithm uses self-normalization to obtain asymptotically normal estimates and valid inference without separately estimating nuisance parameters. The authors report tight confidence intervals from this procedure. It operates fully online with constant space, so its storage requirement does not grow with the amount of data processed.

For median estimation, the paper additionally proves an optimality result using a central limit theorem from Gaussian differential privacy. That optimality claim is specifically associated with the median problem. Mathematical proofs and extensive numerical tests support the method’s validity, combining asymptotic inferential guarantees with an online implementation designed for computational efficiency and minimal storage.
icml-2023-online-local-differential-priv.tldr: The paper gives an online, constant-space method for locally private quantile estimation with asymptotically valid confidence intervals.

paragraphs: Online search in games with hidden information can become expensive because a solver must consider many possible states. Common-knowledge subgame solving includes an especially broad collection of states. Knowledge-limited subgame solving reduces this collection substantially, but its order-1 version, 1-KLSS, does not provide the desired safety.

The authors first introduce Safe-1-KLSS and prove its safety. They then propose Opponent-Limited Subgame Solving, or OLSS, for larger games. OLSS restricts how the opponent can reach a subgame and behave within it, reducing the subgame’s size. Its guarantee is qualified: it preserves some safety in the limit, rather than inheriting an unrestricted safety statement.

In medium-sized poker experiments, both methods run orders of magnitude faster than earlier common-knowledge approaches. OLSS also significantly improves online performance in a two-player Mahjong game too large for those previous methods. The findings show how restricting the search problem can expand practical reach while making the associated safety distinctions explicit.
icml-2023-opponent-limited-online-search.tldr: Safe-1-KLSS and OLSS shrink hidden-information game searches, providing proven safety for the former and qualified limiting safety for the latter.

paragraphs: Quantization-aware training can make weights repeatedly jump between two available numerical levels. These oscillations destabilize training and can harm the resulting model. This paper finds that learnable scaling factors aggravate the problem and that vision transformers face an additional source of oscillation through dependencies between attention’s query and key weights.

The authors propose three corresponding techniques. Statistical weight quantization, StatsQ, improves robustness relative to learnable-scale quantization. Confidence-guided annealing, CGA, freezes high-confidence weights while calming oscillating ones. Query-key reparameterization, QKR, addresses the coupled oscillations in query and key weights and reduces the resulting errors in gradient estimation.

Experiments show reduced weight oscillation and consistent accuracy improvements on ImageNet. For two-bit DeiT-T and DeiT-S, the reported improvements over the previous state of the art are 9.8% and 7.7%, respectively. The findings connect specific sources of quantization instability to targeted training changes, showing substantial benefits in the evaluated low-bit vision transformers.
icml-2023-oscillation-free-quantization-.tldr: Three targeted quantization techniques reduce weight oscillation and substantially improve reported accuracy for low-bit vision transformers.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks spend substantial training time on sparse graph operations. Approximating these operations through sampling is difficult because sparse matrices have irregular numbers of nonzero entries. A sampling choice therefore does not directly translate into a predictable computation cost, and sampling the irregular representation can itself be expensive.

Randomized Sparse Computation manages the accuracy–efficiency trade-off by allocating computation across layers and training epochs. It assigns resources to different sparse operations while keeping total use within a budget. It also caches previously sampled sparse matrices to reduce repeated sampling overhead, and introduces a switching mechanism to improve generalization when training uses approximated operations.

The reported results reach up to an 11.6-fold speedup for an individual sparse operation and a 1.6-fold reduction in end-to-end training time, with almost no accuracy loss. Distinguishing these measurements matters: faster sparse kernels translate into a smaller overall training gain. The approach targets both the arithmetic cost and the overhead involved in making sparse approximation practical.
icml-2023-rsc-accelerate-graph-neural-ne.tldr: RSC accelerates graph neural-network training through budgeted sparse approximations, cached sampling, and a switching mechanism that supports generalization.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether an embodied reinforcement-learning agent can learn simple language indirectly while pursuing a non-language goal. The motivation is that language can become useful for accomplishing tasks even when language prediction is not the training objective. The authors investigate this in an environment where language and task layouts vary.

They construct an office-navigation setting in which the agent must find a particular office. Different buildings place offices in different locations. Each building contains a floor plan with a simple written description of the target’s location, which the agent can inspect visually as an RGB image when it visits the plan.

Agents trained with existing meta-reinforcement-learning algorithms learn to use these descriptions despite receiving no direct language supervision. They generalize to held-out floor-plan layouts and language phrases and quickly reach the correct office. The findings establish this capability within the designed simple-language navigation setting, showing how task success can provide an indirect learning signal for language meaning.
icml-2023-simple-embodied-language-learn.tldr: Meta-reinforcement-learning agents learn to interpret simple visual language through office navigation without direct language supervision.

paragraphs: Graph models often face differences between training and deployment data, such as a mismatch between physics simulations and real experiments. Existing graph domain adaptation methods commonly try to align node representations produced by one shared encoder. This paper examines why that strategy can be inadequate when the underlying graph structure changes.

The authors separate the effects of shifts in graph structure from shifts in node attributes. They identify conditional structure shift and show that current adaptation approaches are provably suboptimal for this type of mismatch. Their proposed structural reweighting method, StruRW, is designed to address the structural problem directly.

Tests cover synthetic graphs, four benchmark datasets, and a high-energy-physics application. StruRW produces significant improvements over baselines when graph-structure shifts are large, and more moderate improvements when node-attribute shifts dominate. The findings indicate that adaptation benefits from accounting for what changed between domains, with the largest reported gains occurring in the structural-shift setting the method targets.
icml-2023-structural-re-weighting-improv.tldr: StruRW addresses graph-structure shifts that representation alignment handles poorly, with especially strong reported gains when structural differences dominate.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning policy that satisfies safety requirements with clean observations can become unsafe when its observations are attacked. Adversarial training can improve robustness, but gathering experience by attacking an acting agent may be costly or dangerous. SAFER addresses this training problem using benign off-policy data, without attacking the agent to collect samples.

Its optimization has two stages. First, convex optimization produces an optimal non-parametric variational policy distribution. Second, supervised learning uses that distribution to improve a parameterized policy robustly. Separating these stages provides a way to guide policy learning with the optimized distribution while using the available benign training data.

Experiments across multiple robot platforms support the method’s ability to learn robust and safe behavior efficiently. The authors report achieving the same reward as on-policy baselines with substantially fewer constraint violations during training. This result links robustness training to the safety of the learning process itself, while retaining the practical advantage of requiring only benign data.
icml-2023-towards-robust-and-safe-reinfo.tldr: SAFER learns robust, safe policies from benign off-policy data and reports fewer training constraint violations at comparable reward.

paragraphs: Small adversarial patches can severely disrupt a vision transformer even when they cover little of an image. The abstract cites earlier attention-based attacks that cover 1–3% of the image and reduce model accuracy to zero. This paper studies how such localized changes affect attention and develops a defense from that understanding.

The authors experimentally observe that adversarial patches are active in only a few layers and become relatively inactive during attention updates. They use these observations to guide a theoretical study of how a small patch can perturb the wider model. The focus is on tracing the attack’s internal behavior rather than considering only its final effect on predictions.

Based on that analysis, the paper proposes a simple, efficient defense and reports correctly detecting more than 95% of adversarial patches. That figure describes patch detection performance. Together, the behavioral observations, theoretical investigation, and detector show how understanding where an attack acts inside a transformer can inform a targeted defense.
icml-2023-understanding-and-defending-pa.tldr: The paper analyzes how small adversarial patches disrupt vision-transformer attention and develops a defense that detects more than 95% of patches.

paragraphs: Probabilistic circuits support efficient probabilistic inference, including marginal-probability calculations. To extend those capabilities to complex data, prior work transfers knowledge from more expressive deep generative models through latent-variable assignments. This paper investigates which properties make that transfer effective, rather than assuming that the most expressive teacher will necessarily be best.

The authors show theoretically and empirically that a probabilistic circuit can outperform its teacher. They therefore study the properties of both teacher and circuit that support good distillation. This analysis leads to a general improvement to the existing latent-variable distillation pipeline, along with additional improvements tailored to particular data types.

On challenging image-modeling benchmarks, the resulting circuits outperform state-of-the-art tractable probabilistic models by a large margin. On ImageNet32, they achieve 4.06 bits per dimension, reported as 0.34 behind variational diffusion models. The findings show that effective distillation depends on the transfer setup and model properties, while preserving the circuit framework’s efficient inference capabilities.
icml-2023-understanding-the-distillation.tldr: The paper explains and improves distillation into probabilistic circuits, showing that a circuit can outperform its generative teacher.
